title: Build Clawbar as a read-only OpenClaw Fleet signal board
description:
## Problem Statement

OpenClaw operators on Omarchy cannot see the current health of their configured Gateway, its Fleet, active Agents, and enabled Automations without leaving the bar and running several commands or opening the full Control UI. Existing status widgets focus on token usage or generic system metrics, while operational failures, stale observations, and upcoming Automation runs remain difficult to distinguish at a glance. A naïve widget that polls text output, probes Nodes directly, or preserves raw CLI data would also make the shell slow and risk exposing Private Content.

## Solution

Clawbar provides a read-only, theme-native Fleet signal board in the Omarchy bar. It connects to exactly one Gateway resolved by OpenClaw, collects only structured Operational Metadata through supported read-only JSON command surfaces, and writes one atomic, versioned snapshot outside QML rendering. The bar summarizes current activity or Attention Items; the keyboard-first panel explains Gateway, Node, Agent, Task Result, Automation, freshness, and setup state without duplicating problems or exposing Private Content.

## User Stories

1. As an Omarchy user, I want Clawbar to appear in the right side of my bar, so that OpenClaw operational state is visible beside other system status indicators.
2. As an OpenClaw operator, I want Clawbar to use the Gateway already selected by OpenClaw, so that I do not configure the same connection twice.
3. As a local Gateway operator, I want Clawbar to resolve the loopback Gateway automatically, so that installation requires no connection setup.
4. As a remote Gateway operator, I want Clawbar to honor OpenClaw's configured remote Gateway, so that it follows my existing trust and routing configuration.
5. As a Node host operator, I want Clawbar to use OpenClaw-owned Gateway connection state, so that a Node host can observe its managing Gateway without a second connection model.
6. As an operator whose Gateway cannot be resolved automatically, I want to choose a Tailscale device as a fallback candidate, so that I can complete setup without entering or storing a Gateway token in Clawbar.
7. As a security-conscious operator, I want a fallback device verified through a supported Gateway command before acceptance, so that an arbitrary reachable device is never treated as a Gateway.
8. As an operator, I want Clawbar to connect to one Gateway rather than probe every Node, so that Fleet size does not multiply network handshakes or CLI startup cost.
9. As an operator, I want Clawbar to show Gateway Setup Required when no Gateway can be resolved, so that setup failure is distinct from an outage.
10. As an operator, I want an Empty Fleet state when a connected Gateway reports no Nodes, so that a valid empty result is distinct from setup failure.
11. As an operator, I want an initial Collecting state, so that normal first collection is not presented as a warning.
12. As an operator, I want No data yet after the bounded first collection fails, so that I know when initial collection did not complete.
13. As an operator, I want the first failed collection from a previously reachable Gateway shown as Unstable, so that a transient failure is visible without immediately declaring an outage.
14. As an operator, I want two consecutive failed collections shown as Offline Gateway, so that persistent loss becomes an Incident.
15. As an operator, I want a reachable Gateway with unavailable Task or Automation metadata shown as Degraded, so that partial data is not confused with an outage.
16. As an operator, I want a reachable Gateway Target without the supported OpenClaw command surface shown as Configuration Error, so that I can distinguish invalid configuration from connection loss.
17. As an operator, I want Node availability to come from the configured Gateway, so that Clawbar never invents Node health from a separate direct probe.
18. As an operator, I want an unavailable Node reported by the Gateway shown as Offline Node, so that affected Fleet members remain visible under their parent tree.
19. As an operator, I want unavailable child metadata to roll up to its parent Node, so that the Fleet tree explains where review is needed.
20. As an operator, I want failed child sections to say unavailable instead of carrying forward old values, so that missing current data cannot masquerade as fresh data.
21. As an operator, I want a stale snapshot shown as a current yellow state after three refresh intervals, so that an old healthy snapshot is never presented as current health.
22. As an operator, I want Last Known Metadata retained after collection loss, so that I keep diagnostic context about the last observed Fleet.
23. As an operator, I want Last Known Metadata to preserve its last observed green, yellow, or red state, so that I can understand what was last seen.
24. As an operator, I want Last Known Metadata visibly dimmed and time-stamped, so that historical state cannot be mistaken for current state.
25. As an operator, I want historical red rows excluded from current Incident and Attention counts, so that old failures do not keep the bar red.
26. As an operator, I want Stale Snapshot yellow to take precedence over historical red, so that the bar communicates that current health is unknown.
27. As an operator, I want Agent Activity limited to Working, Waiting, or Idle, so that it describes only present work.
28. As an operator, I want Idle Agents shown without an activity dot or redundant Idle label, so that inactive rows stay quiet.
29. As an operator, I want the most recent Task Result shown separately from Agent Activity, so that current work and completed outcomes are not conflated.
30. As an operator, I want a Working Agent to be allowed to show a previous Failed Task Result, so that history remains accurate without declaring the Agent failed now.
31. As an operator, I want a regular Task failure kept out of Node and Gateway health, so that one task outcome does not become an operational Incident.
32. As an operator, I want enabled Automations to show their name, next run, last result, and consecutive failure count, so that scheduled work is glanceable.
33. As an operator, I want successful and failed Automation results shown distinctly, so that the last outcome is immediately legible.
34. As an operator, I want an Automation Failure to become an immediate Incident, so that confirmed scheduled-work failure does not wait for another poll.
35. As an operator, I want disabled Automations to remain visible with their name and last-run time, so that forgotten configuration can still be discovered.
36. As an operator, I want disabled Automations dimmed and marked Disabled, so that they cannot be confused with unavailable or failed Automations.
37. As an operator, I want disabled Automations excluded from Attention Items and Incidents, so that intentional inactivity creates no warning.
38. As an operator, I want Gateway-level Attention Items above the Fleet tree when necessary, so that setup, reachability, and freshness problems are explained first.
39. As an operator, I want Node and Automation problems represented once inside the Fleet tree, so that a separate attention summary does not duplicate the same failure.
40. As an operator, I want red states ordered before yellow states within their natural tree level, so that confirmed failures take visual priority.
41. As an operator, I want the bar count to mean Working Agent count during healthy operation, so that current activity is visible without opening the panel.
42. As an operator, I want the bar count to mean current Attention Item count during yellow or red operation, so that problem scale is visible at a glance.
43. As an operator, I want simultaneous Incident starts grouped into one desktop notification, so that one collection cannot create a notification storm.
44. As an operator, I want simultaneous recoveries grouped into one desktop notification, so that recovery is concise.
45. As an operator, I want each Incident notified once per desktop login, so that repeated collections in the same state remain quiet.
46. As an operator, I want a confirmed recovery notified once, so that I know the problem ended without reopening the panel.
47. As an operator, I want removing a monitored target or disabling an Automation to end monitoring silently, so that configuration changes are not falsely described as recovery.
48. As a keyboard user, I want `j`, `k`, and arrow keys to move visible selection, so that the panel is usable without a pointer.
49. As a keyboard user, I want Enter to expand or collapse a Node, so that I can control information density.
50. As a keyboard user, I want `r` to request an immediate non-blocking collection, so that I can refresh without freezing the shell.
51. As a keyboard user, I want Escape to close the panel, so that navigation follows Omarchy conventions.
52. As an operator, I want `o` on a Gateway or Agent context to open the official Control UI through OpenClaw's safe handoff, so that Clawbar never handles an admin token.
53. As an operator, I want `o` on an Automation to open read-only recent-run history for the same Gateway, so that I can investigate without mutating the job.
54. As an operator, I want Node summary rows before expanded detail, so that the Fleet remains scannable at panel width.
55. As an operator, I want relative times in the tree and an absolute local time in selected-row detail, so that urgency and exact timing are both available.
56. As an Omarchy theme user, I want Clawbar to use installed semantic theme tokens, so that it belongs to every Omarchy theme.
57. As a user with color-vision or contrast needs, I want state communicated by text strength, labels, dot treatment, and timestamps as well as color, so that color is never the only signal.
58. As a reduced-motion user, I want the panel understandable without animation, so that motion is optional rather than informational.
59. As an operator sharing my screen, I want task instructions, message bodies, destinations, account identifiers, host/IP/instance identifiers, and raw errors absent, so that Clawbar does not expose Private Content.
60. As an operator, I want raw CLI responses discarded after bounded parsing, so that the snapshot contains only Operational Metadata.
61. As an operator, I want collector work outside QML rendering, so that a slow Gateway cannot make the shell unresponsive.
62. As an operator, I want an atomic snapshot replacement, so that QML never reads partially written JSON.
63. As an operator, I want collection bounded to twelve seconds and overlapping refreshes coalesced, so that failed collection cannot accumulate background processes.
64. As an operator, I want a thirty-second default refresh interval configurable from fifteen to three hundred seconds, so that I can balance freshness and Gateway load.
65. As an operator, I want disabling or removing Clawbar to stop future collection immediately, so that no orphan timer or collector behavior remains.
66. As a Marketplace user, I want installation and removal to use normal Omarchy plugin commands, so that no separate systemd setup is required.
67. As a Marketplace user, I want dependencies and supported OpenClaw release requirements documented, so that compatibility is predictable.
68. As a developer, I want sanitized fictional fixtures and a non-user-facing demo path, so that every accepted state can be reproduced without copying real OpenClaw data.
69. As a developer, I want the twelve accepted prototype scenarios preserved as decision evidence, so that the QML implementation can be checked against reviewed behavior.
70. As a reviewer, I want Clawbar to remain read-only end to end, so that no UI action can create, edit, delete, retry, cancel, or otherwise mutate OpenClaw work.

## Implementation Decisions

1. **Product contract.** Clawbar is “A read-only OpenClaw fleet status view for the Omarchy bar.” The UI, notifications, README, and Marketplace copy use English and the domain vocabulary defined for Gateway, Fleet, Node, Agent Activity, Task Result, Automation, Attention Item, Incident, and Last Known Metadata.

2. **One-Gateway architecture.** Clawbar connects to exactly one Gateway and never directly to Nodes. The Gateway is the sole source of Fleet, Node, Agent, Task, and Automation metadata. This is a clean replacement for the earlier direct multi-Node and SSH fan-out model.

3. **Gateway resolution module.** Resolution first delegates to OpenClaw's existing local configuration and CLI behavior: local mode selects loopback, remote mode selects the configured remote URL, and Node-host state may identify the managing Gateway. Only when OpenClaw cannot resolve a Gateway may the setup UI enumerate Tailscale devices. A selected device remains a Gateway Target candidate until a supported read-only Gateway JSON command succeeds. Clawbar stores no Gateway token or password.

4. **Supported command adapter.** The initial supported release is the current stable OpenClaw contract validated against `2026.7.1-2`. The adapter uses structured JSON and meaningful exit codes only. Gateway health uses a bounded RPC-requiring JSON probe without `--deep`; Node state uses the Gateway-backed Node status JSON surface; general status and task JSON surfaces provide only fields proven to belong to the configured Gateway; Automation collection uses the stable cron list JSON surface while all product vocabulary remains Automation. Text matching, merged stderr parsing, swallowed exit codes, internal SQLite/JSONL reads, and continuous deep probes are prohibited. If a supported surface cannot provide a field, that section becomes unavailable or Degraded rather than inferred from unrelated local data.

5. **Collector module.** Replace the Bash scaffold with one Python 3 standard-library collector. Its external interface accepts resolved settings through environment/arguments, invokes only the command adapter, enforces the twelve-second whole-collection deadline, coalesces overlapping requests, reduces raw responses to Operational Metadata, advances state, writes the atomic snapshot, and emits grouped transition notifications. It has no third-party Python package dependency.

6. **Scheduling module.** A lightweight Quickshell service entry point owns an immediate and repeating timer. The default interval is thirty seconds and follows the configured fifteen-to-three-hundred-second value. It starts the separate collector process asynchronously and does not start a second collector while one is running. Manual refresh uses the same scheduler. The systemd units and manual install/remove lifecycle are removed.

7. **Snapshot interface.** QML and tests consume one versioned JSON snapshot. The interface includes schema version, generation time, configured refresh interval, current collection result, resolved Gateway Target label and source, Gateway state and last successful time, consecutive full-failure count, current or Last Known Fleet, Node state, Agent Activity, Task Result, enabled and disabled Automation metadata, Attention rollups, and non-sensitive generalized error codes. It contains no raw command output or Private Content. Runtime snapshot and Incident deduplication state are per-login data rather than durable user data.

8. **Atomicity and freshness.** The collector writes a temporary file in the destination directory, flushes it, and renames it over the prior snapshot. Snapshot age greater than three configured refresh intervals produces Stale Snapshot. A stale snapshot is the current yellow state and suppresses historical red from current Incident and Attention counts.

9. **Collection state model.** Collecting is neutral during the first bounded attempt; No data yet is yellow after the first attempt yields no valid snapshot. A previously successful Gateway becomes Unstable after one full collection failure and Offline after two consecutive full failures. A reachable but unsupported Gateway Target is Configuration Error immediately. A reachable Gateway with unavailable Task or Automation metadata is Degraded. Successful collection resets the consecutive failure count.

10. **Last Known Metadata.** Full collection failure may retain the last successful Fleet as historical context. Every retained row preserves its last observed state but is dimmed, marked Last known, and given a relative timestamp. Historical rows are excluded from current counts and cannot start or extend an Incident. Failed sections within an otherwise current partial collection are not carried forward.

11. **Agent and Task model.** Agent Activity is present state only: Working, Waiting, or Idle. Idle has no activity dot or redundant label. Task Result is the most recent completed outcome and time, independent of Agent Activity. A Failed Task Result is display-only and never rolls up to Node or Gateway health.

12. **Automation model.** Enabled Automations show name, next run, last result, and consecutive failure count. Current success is healthy; current failure is an immediate Automation Failure. Disabled Automations remain visible with name and last-run time, muted text, a dotted muted indicator, and Disabled; they create no Attention Item or Incident.

13. **Tree aggregation.** Gateway-level Attention Items may appear before the Fleet tree. Node and Automation conditions remain in the tree and roll up to their parent Node. They are never copied into a second attention list. Regular Task failure never rolls up. Bar severity uses current state only, with red above yellow.

14. **Notification module.** The collector, not QML, compares per-login Incident state and emits notifications through the desktop notification system. Incident starts and recoveries discovered in one collection are grouped separately into at most one failure and one recovery notification. Repeated polls are silent. Removal from monitoring ends the Incident without recovery notification. A new desktop login may notify a still-current Incident again.

15. **Panel and bar module.** The accepted Fleet signal-board design is the visual source of truth: a compact claw mark plus state point in the bar, a thin Fleet rail, Node connection points, quiet dense rows, and progressive Node disclosure. During healthy operation the bar count is Working Agents; during current yellow/red operation it is Attention Items. Empty Fleet retains a muted setup icon. Stale yellow takes precedence over historical red.

16. **Status legend semantics.** Healthy Node and successful Automation use the theme's green; current confirmed failures use red; Waiting and needs-review operational states share yellow but remain semantically distinct through labels and row context. Last Known Metadata uses reduced text strength while retaining the last observed state indicator. Disabled Automation uses muted dotted treatment. Idle uses no dot. The implementation never claims one color has one universal domain meaning.

17. **Theme interface.** QML consumes Omarchy semantic tokens rather than fixed colors. Required verification themes are white, catppuccin-latte, flexoki-light, and vantablack. Red/yellow distinction, focus, text hierarchy, historical dimming, and disabled treatment must survive all four. Keyboard focus uses accent; Last Known Metadata uses muted treatment. State always includes non-color information.

18. **Interaction interface.** `j`/`k` and arrow keys move selection, Enter expands or collapses the selected Node, `r` requests a non-blocking refresh, and Escape closes the panel. `o` uses OpenClaw's official dashboard handoff for Gateway/Agent contexts and opens read-only recent Automation run history for an Automation. There is no direct Node SSH action in the one-Gateway model.

19. **Privacy module.** Parsing is allowlist-based. Only defined Operational Metadata crosses the snapshot seam. Generalized error codes may distinguish timeout, authentication/setup, unsupported surface, invalid JSON, and unavailable section; raw stderr and raw errors are discarded. Development fixtures are generated only through a sanitizer or authored fictionally, and are checked for real names, hosts, accounts, destinations, paths, tokens, task text, and message text before commit.

20. **Marketplace contract.** The plugin uses a globally unique non-reserved identifier under the authenticated GitHub owner namespace, the right bar section, category Widgets, tags `ai`, `bar`, and `quickshell`, and MIT licensing. The repository root contains the manifest, installation/removal documentation, license, dependencies, and a polished preview. The manifest declares both the bar-widget and service entry points needed for normal Omarchy lifecycle management.

21. **Clean cutover.** Remove the minimal text-matching collector, the sixty-second systemd timer, manual systemd installation instructions, the minimal bar-only snapshot reader, old identifier/copy, and any claim that the scaffold implements the accepted state model. There are no compatibility aliases or dual collectors after migration.

## Testing Decisions

- A good automated test exercises externally observable collector behavior through the same command interface used by Quickshell. Tests do not call internal parser/state helpers or assert implementation structure.
- The single automated test seam is the collector executable. Each test provides fake `openclaw`, optional fake `tailscale`, and fake notification commands plus isolated XDG runtime/config state; it runs the collector and inspects only the resulting snapshot, exit behavior, and notification record.
- The command fakes return representative JSON and exit codes. They never use real OpenClaw state, credentials, hostnames, task text, message text, or destinations.
- Contract cases cover automatic local, remote, and Node-host Gateway resolution; unresolved setup; Tailscale candidate listing; candidate verification success and failure; and refusal to accept an unverified candidate.
- Health cases prove that successful RPC JSON is healthy, one full failure is Unstable, two are Offline, partial section failure is Degraded, and successful recovery resets failures. Text such as `invalid token`, `connection broken`, or unrelated `ok` substrings must never produce healthy state.
- Command cases prove that the collector uses structured JSON, honors non-zero exits and deadlines, never relies on merged stderr, and never invokes continuous deep status probing.
- Snapshot cases cover schema version, generated time, refresh interval, Gateway source, per-section freshness, Last Known Metadata, no carry-forward for partially failed sections, current counts, and stale-at-three-interval behavior.
- Atomicity is tested behaviorally by repeated reads during replacement; every observed file must be either the complete prior snapshot or complete next snapshot, never partial JSON.
- Agent cases cover Working/Waiting/Idle, no Idle activity marker input, independent previous Failed Task Result, and exclusion of regular Task failures from Attention and Incident state.
- Automation cases cover enabled success, enabled failure, consecutive failure count, disabled visibility, and disabled exclusion from Attention and Incident state.
- Aggregation cases cover Node rollup, Automation rollup, no duplicate attention list, Gateway-level placement, red-over-yellow severity, Working count in healthy state, and Attention count in warning/failure state.
- Notification cases cover one failure notification per Incident per login, one recovery notification, grouped simultaneous starts, grouped simultaneous recoveries, silence on repeated polls, silence when a target is removed, and notification reset across a new login.
- Privacy cases seed every prohibited Private Content field and sentinel string into fake command output and prove none appears in snapshot, notification, stdout, or committed fixture output.
- Lifecycle cases prove that service disable/remove stops scheduling, a running collector exits within the deadline, manual refresh coalesces with an active collection, and no systemd timer remains required.
- QML does not gain a second automated test interface. The actual Omarchy shell is the behavioral UI verification surface: load sanitized snapshots representing the twelve accepted prototype scenarios and verify bar/panel behavior, keyboard control, focus, expansion, stale/history distinction, and action dispatch.
- Visual verification runs the actual shell against white, catppuccin-latte, flexoki-light, and vantablack at narrow and wide panel widths, with reduced motion enabled once. It checks red/yellow distinction, historical and disabled treatment, no overflow, responsive shell interaction, and no console errors.
- Responsiveness verification runs collection against delayed and failing command fakes while repeatedly opening and navigating the actual panel; rendering must remain immediate because QML reads only the cached snapshot.
- Installation verification uses normal Omarchy add, validate, enable, disable, update, and remove flows. Removal must leave no active timer, collector, or notification behavior.
- Prior art is the accepted self-contained Fleet signal-board prototype with twelve reviewed scenarios, Omarchy's built-in bar-widget/service patterns, and `omarchy plugin validate`. The repository currently has no automated test suite, so the collector executable seam is the first and only automated seam introduced.

## Out of Scope

- Token, quota, credit, or cost metering.
- Reimplementing the OpenClaw Control UI.
- Creating, editing, deleting, enabling, disabling, retrying, cancelling, or otherwise mutating Tasks, Nodes, Agents, or Automations.
- Reading OpenClaw's internal SQLite, JSONL, transcript, memory, workspace, credential, or plugin storage directly.
- Persisting Gateway administrator tokens, passwords, SSH keys, or other credentials.
- Connecting directly to Fleet Nodes or running one SSH/OpenClaw probe per Node.
- Managing SSH tunnels or exposing a remote Control UI.
- Supporting Claude, Codex, Herdr, Boomux, or a generic multi-agent framework.
- Requiring Prometheus, OpenTelemetry, a database, a daemon framework, or third-party Python packages.
- Polling `status --deep` or channel health probes continuously.
- Supporting legacy/beta command contracts beyond the declared current stable OpenClaw release.
- Inferring missing per-Node Agent or Task data from unrelated local files or timestamps.
- Displaying task instructions, message bodies, destinations, account identifiers, raw errors, host/IP/instance identifiers, or other Private Content.
- A user-facing demo mode.
- UI localization in the competition release.
- A second automated QML testing interface or tests that assert internal helper functions.
- Shipping systemd units or requiring manual service installation.

## Further Notes

- The accepted HTML prototype is decision evidence, not production code. Its twelve scenarios, status legend, tree aggregation, freshness treatment, and four-theme checks are the visual reference for implementation.
- The current scaffold passes structural plugin validation but does not satisfy this spec. Its collector polls deep text output, merges stderr, discards exit status, performs unsafe substring health matching, emits an underspecified snapshot, and cannot represent Fleet, freshness, Last Known Metadata, or the accepted state model. The current QML reads only that minimal snapshot, polls at sixty seconds, and has no accepted panel.
- Structural validation is necessary but not behavioral proof. Completion requires the collector contract tests plus the actual Omarchy surface checks described above.
- Marketplace submission requires a public GitHub root repository, permanent unique identifier, root manifest, installation and removal instructions, root license, dependency documentation, and optional preview. Use category `Widgets` and tags `ai`, `bar`, `quickshell`.
- Competition submission is due 2026-08-24 at 09:00 CEST, so implementation tickets should preserve a tracer-bullet path: correct structured collection and snapshot first, then one real bar/panel path, then full state/notification/theme coverage, then Marketplace completion.
